title: The Miraculous Birth of Jesus
subtitle: The virgin birth in the Quran and the Gospels — one miracle, two conclusions
summary: Islam and Christianity both affirm that Mary conceived Jesus while a virgin. Christianity often treats the miracle as fitting the incarnation; the Quran treats it as a sign of God's creative power. Adam had neither father nor mother, yet is not divine. Jesus's miraculous birth therefore proves the greatness of God and the special mission of Jesus, not that Jesus is God.

sections.title: The Virgin Birth: A Sign of God, Not Proof That Jesus Is God
sections.body: Islam and Christianity both affirm that Mary conceived Jesus while a virgin. Christianity often treats the miracle as fitting the incarnation; the Quran treats it as a sign of God's creative power. Adam had neither father nor mother, yet is not divine. Jesus's miraculous birth therefore proves the greatness of God and the special mission of Jesus, not that Jesus is God.

sections.title: A Rare Point of Deep Agreement
sections.body:
Discussions between Muslims and Christians often concentrate on the points of disagreement: the Trinity, the crucifixion, the nature of scripture. It is easy to forget that on one of the most astonishing claims in either scripture, the two faiths stand together. Both affirm that Jesus was conceived in the womb of a virgin, by the direct action of God, without any human father.

A quick definition helps at the start. "Virgin birth" — more precisely, virginal conception — means that Mary conceived Jesus while remaining a virgin: no man was involved at any point. This is not a fringe opinion in either religion. It is stated plainly in the Quran and in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, confessed in the historic Christian creeds, and affirmed by Muslim scholarship across all schools.

The Quran's regard for Mary goes further than many readers expect. She is the only woman referred to by her own name anywhere in the Quran — other women, such as the wife of Pharaoh or the mother of Moses, are identified by their relationships. The Quran includes a chapter bearing her name: Surah Maryam (chapter 19). Reading the two annunciation accounts side by side reveals striking similarities before raising the question that divides the two faiths: what does a miraculous birth prove?

sections.title: The Real Question: What Does the Miracle Mean?
sections.body:
Both scriptures say it did, and both faith communities have always believed it. The question is what the miracle means.

For Christian tradition, the virgin birth belongs to a larger claim: that the child conceived in Mary was the eternal Son of God taking on human nature — the doctrine known as the incarnation. On this reading, the miraculous conception is the doorway through which God entered the world as a man.

Islam draws a different conclusion from the same event. In the Quran, the virgin birth is a sign — in Arabic, an ayah — of God's unlimited power to create. God created Adam with no father and no mother; He creates every other human being from two parents; and He created Jesus from a mother alone. When God decrees a thing, He says "Be," and it is. A miraculous origin, in this reading, makes Jesus a uniquely honored prophet and Messiah — not a divine son.

So the real dispute is a dispute about inference: does the miracle show that God became man, or that God needs no means at all to create a man? Keeping that question in view will make the comparison easier to follow.

sections.title: The Sources and Their Setting
sections.body:
Matthew and Luke contain the New Testament's infancy narratives. They agree that Mary conceived Jesus before living with a husband, though their surrounding details and genealogies differ. The Quran gives its own detailed account in Surahs Al Imran and Maryam, centering Mary's faith, the angelic announcement, and God's command.

The historical method cannot verify a virginal conception directly. The question is therefore bound to the reliability of revelation and the meaning each scripture gives the miracle.

sections.title: The Annunciation in the Quran
sections.body:
The angel tells Mary that God gives her "a word from Him" named the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary (Quran 3:45). When she asks how she can have a child, the answer is not that God will become her child, but that God creates whatever He wills: "When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is" (Quran 3:47).

Surah Maryam repeats the same point. The spirit appears as a man, Mary protests her chastity, and she is told that the birth will be a sign and mercy (Quran 19:17-21). After the birth, the infant Jesus declares, "I am the servant of Allah ... He has made me a prophet" (Quran 19:30).

The Quran thus joins miracle and servanthood. Jesus is extraordinary because God chose and created him by command, not because God entered creation.

sections.title: The Annunciation in Matthew and Luke
sections.body:
Matthew 1:18-23 and Luke 1 also affirm conception by the Holy Spirit before Mary and Joseph came together. Luke records the angel calling Jesus Messiah and saying that he will be called Son of the Most High. Christians read these titles through incarnation and divine sonship.

Muslims respect the Gospel witness to Mary's chastity and the miracle while reading "son" in its biblical setting, where chosen servants and kings can be called sons of God. A miraculous origin alone cannot establish deity: Adam's creation is still more unusual, and Luke itself calls Adam "son of God" (Luke 3:38) without making Adam divine.

sections.title: One Miracle, Two Conclusions
sections.body:
The agreement is profound: Mary is chaste, conception is miraculous, Jesus is Messiah, and the event is God's sign. The disagreement concerns what follows.

Christian theology reads the virgin birth as appropriate to God the Son becoming human. The Quran states the lesson explicitly: Jesus is like Adam, created by God's command (Quran 3:59). The miracle displays the Creator's freedom from ordinary causes. It does not turn the created child into the Creator.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions
sections.body:
"Muslims deny the virgin birth." This is perhaps the most common misconception of all, and it is exactly backwards. The Quran teaches the virginal conception explicitly and defends Mary's chastity emphatically — she is "the one who guarded her chastity" (Quran 21:91). A Muslim who denied the virgin birth would be denying the plain text of the Quran.

"The Quran only rejects a crude idea of sonship that Christians never held." Mainstream Christian doctrine does deny any physical fatherhood on God's part, and that distinction should be stated clearly. But the Quran's rejection is broader: it denies that God has offspring in any sense, physical or metaphysical, because attributing a son to God compromises His absolute self-sufficiency and uniqueness. The disagreement is real; it is just not the cartoon version.

"Islam diminishes Mary." The opposite is true. She is the only woman named in the Quran, a chapter of the Quran carries her name, and the Quran calls her chosen "above the women of the worlds" (Quran 3:42) and a model of devotion for believers (Quran 66:12).

"A child with no human father must be the Son of God." The Quran answers this directly with the case of Adam (Quran 3:59), who had no father and no mother. Careful Christian theology agrees that the virgin birth alone does not establish divinity — it locates Jesus's sonship in his eternal nature, not in the mode of his conception. So both traditions reject the inference here; they part ways over the separate claim of eternal sonship.

"The Quran and the Gospels disagree about who visited Mary." Luke names Gabriel; the Quran says God sent "Our Spirit," who appeared to her as "a well-proportioned man" (Quran 19:17), and Muslim commentary has overwhelmingly identified this Spirit as Gabriel. This is convergence, not contradiction.

"The Holy Spirit means the same thing in both accounts." In Christian doctrine the Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity. In Islamic understanding, the Spirit associated with Jesus's conception is the angel Gabriel, a created being who carries God's command. The narrative role is the same; the theology behind the term differs — a good example of why definitions matter in comparative reading.

sections.title: A Sign Pointing to God
sections.body:
The virgin birth is a reason for Muslims to love Mary, honor Jesus, and glorify God. It does not divide God's oneness. The child who was born miraculously identifies himself in the Quran as God's servant and prophet.

Islam preserves both sides of the truth: Jesus is unlike ordinary people in his birth and mission, yet he remains fully human and dependent on God. This allows the miracle to lead where every prophetic sign should lead—to worship of the One who performed it.

sections.title: Key Takeaways: What the Virgin Birth Means
sections.body: The virgin birth is common ground between Islam and Christianity, but the Quran states its meaning with unusual clarity. God created Jesus by command, just as He created Adam in an even more extraordinary way. Jesus is therefore a sign from God and a true Messiah, not God Himself.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Do Muslims believe Jesus was born of a virgin?
A: Yes, without qualification. The Quran states that Mary conceived Jesus while no man had touched her (Quran 3:47; 19:20), and belief in the virgin birth has been the unanimous position of Islamic scholarship. Denying it would contradict the plain text of the Quran.

Q: Why is Mary so important in Islam?
A: Mary (Maryam) is the only woman mentioned by name in the Quran, and Surah 19 is named after her. The Quran says God chose her and purified her above the women of the worlds (Quran 3:42) and presents her as a model of chastity, faith, and devotion for believers (Quran 66:12).

Q: If Jesus had no father, doesn't that make him the Son of God?
A: The Quran answers this with the example of Adam (Quran 3:59): Adam had neither father nor mother, yet he was a created human being. A miraculous origin shows God's power to create as He wills; it does not make the created one divine. Notably, classical Christian theology also holds that Jesus's divine sonship is eternal rather than caused by the virgin birth, so both traditions agree the miracle alone does not establish divinity.

Q: Who was the spirit or angel that appeared to Mary?
A: Luke names the angel Gabriel. The Quran says God sent 'Our Spirit,' who appeared to Mary in the form of a man (Quran 19:17), and Muslim commentators have overwhelmingly identified this Spirit as Gabriel. The two accounts converge on the same messenger.

Q: Do the Quran and the Bible describe the same annunciation?
A: The parallels are striking: an angel announces a son to a virgin, she asks how this can be when no man has touched her, and the answer appeals to God's power. Both accounts also call Jesus the Messiah and exalt Mary among women. The two faiths differ mainly in the theological conclusion they draw, not in the event they describe.

Q: Does the Quran call Jesus the Messiah?
A: Yes. In Quran 3:45 the angels announce him as 'the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary,' distinguished in this world and the Hereafter. Islam affirms Jesus as the Messiah sent to Israel while understanding that title as a mark of his mission, not of divinity.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
Selected sources and further reading:

- **Jesus in the Qur'an** — Geoffrey Parrinder. A respectful survey by a Christian scholar of religion covering the Quranic passages about Jesus and Mary.
- **The Muslim Jesus: Sayings and Stories in Islamic Literature** — Tarif Khalidi. How Jesus is remembered and quoted in the wider Islamic tradition beyond the Quran.
- **The Islamic Jesus** — Mustafa Akyol. An accessible modern discussion of the Quranic Jesus and Mary in conversation with Jewish and Christian views.
- **The Birth of the Messiah** — Raymond E. Brown. A classic Christian scholarly commentary on the infancy narratives of Matthew and Luke.
- **The Qur'an and the Bible: Text and Commentary** — Gabriel Said Reynolds. A verse-by-verse academic comparison of Quranic passages with their biblical parallels, including the Mary narratives.

quranVerses.arabic: وَإِذْ قَالَتِ ٱلْمَلَٰٓئِكَةُ يَٰمَرْيَمُ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ ٱصْطَفَىٰكِ وَطَهَّرَكِ وَٱصْطَفَىٰكِ عَلَىٰ نِسَآءِ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ
quranVerses.translation: And [mention] when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you and chosen you above the women of the worlds.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: إِذْ قَالَتِ ٱلْمَلَٰٓئِكَةُ يَٰمَرْيَمُ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُبَشِّرُكِ بِكَلِمَةٍۢ مِّنْهُ ٱسْمُهُ ٱلْمَسِيحُ عِيسَى ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ وَجِيهًۭا فِى ٱلدُّنْيَا وَٱلْءَاخِرَةِ وَمِنَ ٱلْمُقَرَّبِينَ
quranVerses.translation: [And mention] when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him, whose name will be the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary - distinguished in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near [to Allah].
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَيُكَلِّمُ ٱلنَّاسَ فِى ٱلْمَهْدِ وَكَهْلًۭا وَمِنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ
quranVerses.translation: He will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity and will be of the righteous."
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: قَالَتْ رَبِّ أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لِى وَلَدٌۭ وَلَمْ يَمْسَسْنِى بَشَرٌۭ ۖ قَالَ كَذَٰلِكِ ٱللَّهُ يَخْلُقُ مَا يَشَآءُ ۚ إِذَا قَضَىٰٓ أَمْرًۭا فَإِنَّمَا يَقُولُ لَهُۥ كُن فَيَكُونُ
quranVerses.translation: She said, "My Lord, how will I have a child when no man has touched me?" [The angel] said, "Such is Allah; He creates what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَٱذْكُرْ فِى ٱلْكِتَٰبِ مَرْيَمَ إِذِ ٱنتَبَذَتْ مِنْ أَهْلِهَا مَكَانًۭا شَرْقِيًّۭا
quranVerses.translation: And mention, [O Muhammad], in the Book [the story of] Mary, when she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: فَٱتَّخَذَتْ مِن دُونِهِمْ حِجَابًۭا فَأَرْسَلْنَآ إِلَيْهَا رُوحَنَا فَتَمَثَّلَ لَهَا بَشَرًۭا سَوِيًّۭا
quranVerses.translation: And she took, in seclusion from them, a screen. Then We sent to her Our Angel, and he represented himself to her as a well-proportioned man.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: قَالَتْ إِنِّىٓ أَعُوذُ بِٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ مِنكَ إِن كُنتَ تَقِيًّۭا
quranVerses.translation: She said, "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, [so leave me], if you should be fearing of Allah."
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: قَالَ إِنَّمَآ أَنَا۠ رَسُولُ رَبِّكِ لِأَهَبَ لَكِ غُلَٰمًۭا زَكِيًّۭا
quranVerses.translation: He said, "I am only the messenger of your Lord to give you [news of] a pure boy."
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: قَالَتْ أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لِى غُلَٰمٌۭ وَلَمْ يَمْسَسْنِى بَشَرٌۭ وَلَمْ أَكُ بَغِيًّۭا
quranVerses.translation: She said, "How can I have a boy while no man has touched me and I have not been unchaste?"
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: قَالَ كَذَٰلِكِ قَالَ رَبُّكِ هُوَ عَلَىَّ هَيِّنٌۭ ۖ وَلِنَجْعَلَهُۥٓ ءَايَةًۭ لِّلنَّاسِ وَرَحْمَةًۭ مِّنَّا ۚ وَكَانَ أَمْرًۭا مَّقْضِيًّۭا
quranVerses.translation: He said, "Thus [it will be]; your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me, and We will make him a sign to the people and a mercy from Us. And it is a matter [already] decreed.' "
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَٱلَّتِىٓ أَحْصَنَتْ فَرْجَهَا فَنَفَخْنَا فِيهَا مِن رُّوحِنَا وَجَعَلْنَٰهَا وَٱبْنَهَآ ءَايَةًۭ لِّلْعَٰلَمِينَ
quranVerses.translation: And [mention] the one who guarded her chastity, so We blew into her [garment] through Our angel [Gabriel], and We made her and her son a sign for the worlds.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَمَرْيَمَ ٱبْنَتَ عِمْرَٰنَ ٱلَّتِىٓ أَحْصَنَتْ فَرْجَهَا فَنَفَخْنَا فِيهِ مِن رُّوحِنَا وَصَدَّقَتْ بِكَلِمَٰتِ رَبِّهَا وَكُتُبِهِۦ وَكَانَتْ مِنَ ٱلْقَٰنِتِينَ
quranVerses.translation: And [the example of] Mary, the daughter of 'Imran, who guarded her chastity, so We blew into [her garment] through Our angel, and she believed in the words of her Lord and His scriptures and was of the devoutly obedient.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: إِنَّ مَثَلَ عِيسَىٰ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ كَمَثَلِ ءَادَمَ ۖ خَلَقَهُۥ مِن تُرَابٍۢ ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُۥ كُن فَيَكُونُ
quranVerses.translation: Indeed, the example of Jesus to Allah is like that of Adam. He created Him from dust; then He said to him, "Be," and he was.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: قَالَ إِنِّى عَبْدُ ٱللَّهِ ءَاتَىٰنِىَ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ وَجَعَلَنِى نَبِيًّۭا
quranVerses.translation: [Jesus] said, "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

bibleVerses.text: Now the birth of Jesus Christ was like this: After his mother, Mary, was engaged to Joseph, before they came together, she was found pregnant by the Holy Spirit. Joseph, her husband, being a righteous man, and not willing to make her a public example, intended to put her away secretly. But when he thought about these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, “Joseph, son of David, don’t be afraid to take to yourself Mary, your wife, for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit. She shall give birth to a son. You shall call his name Jesus, for it is he who shall save his people from their sins.” Now all this has happened, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet, saying, “Behold, the virgin shall be with child, and shall give birth to a son. They shall call his name Immanuel”; which is, being interpreted, “God with us.”

Now in the sixth month, the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee, named Nazareth, to a virgin pledged to be married to a man whose name was Joseph, of David’s house. The virgin’s name was Mary. Having come in, the angel said to her, “Rejoice, you highly favored one! The Lord is with you. Blessed are you among women!” But when she saw him, she was greatly troubled at the saying, and considered what kind of salutation this might be. The angel said to her, “Don’t be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb, and give birth to a son, and will call his name ‘Jesus.’ He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give him the throne of his father, David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever. There will be no end to his Kingdom.” Mary said to the angel, “How can this be, seeing I am a virgin?” The angel answered her, “The Holy Spirit will come on you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore also the holy one who is born from you will be called the Son of God.
Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin will conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
